chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Muhammad from Salih ibn Abi Hammad, all from al-Wasshash, from Ahmad ibn A'idh, from Abi Khadija, from Mu'la ibn Khunays, from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man said to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), 'O Messenger of Allah, teach me.' He said, 'Go and do not be angry.' The man said, 'I am content with that,' and went to his people. He found that a conflict had arisen among them; they had lined up in rows and put on their weapons. When he saw that, he put on his weapon, then stood with them. Then he remembered the words of the Messenger of Allah, 'Do not be angry,' so he threw down the weapon and came walking to the people who were the enemies of his people, saying, 'O you all! Whatever injury, or killing, or a blow without lasting effect was from you, upon me is (the compensation) from my wealth; I will fulfill it for you.' The people said, 'So whatever it was, it is for you; we are more entitled to it than you are.' He said, 'So the people reconciled and the anger departed.'
He said, 'So the people reconciled and the anger departed.'
ai.seo_question: What is the concise advice the Prophet gave for controlling anger and resolving conflict?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated in al-Kafi, highlights the Prophet’s (peace be upon him and his family) concise advice of 'Do not be angry' as a comprehensive key to success, a concept often linked to the famous narration of Imam Ali (peace be upon him). The narrative illustrates the practical application of this virtue in tribal warfare, where self-restraint and financial compensation for minor injuries effectively neutralize hostility and secure peace. It underscores the Shia scholarly view that mastering anger is not merely emotional control but a strategic tool for social harmony and conflict resolution.
